newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany will meet EMU entry criteria -- Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Germany will meet EMU entry criteria -- Waigel.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Sunday Germany would qualify for Europe's single currency without any softening of the entry criteria.

His insistence on Germany's ability to do so followed statements by several of the country's senior figures that a looser interpretation of entry rules would be preferable to a delay to the euro project.

"You will see, Germany will make the deficit criteria," Waigel told journalists at a weekend meeting of the junior wing of his Christian Social Union (CSU), Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).

Waigel denied there was any discussion in his party of delaying economic and monetary union (EMU) beyond its scheduled 1999 launch and promised Germany would fulfil the Maastricht goal of budget deficit at three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

But many economists predict slow economic growth and soaring unemployment will mean Germany cannot hit that target precisely, prompting some senior figures to call for relaxing criteria for the deficit target rather than a delay.
"The convergence criteria are not mathematical (goals), but rather psychological," Karl Lamers, CDU foreign policy spokesman told Berlin's Tagesspiegel newspaper in an interview.
"Structural reforms are decisive for the durability of stability policies and not, as some want the impression to be, the exact decimal point fulfilment of the three percent criterion," he said.

Martin Kohlhaussen, president of the Federal Association of German Banks, agreed. He told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung Germany should enter the first wave of EMU in 1999 even if its deficit was as high as 3.3 percent of GDP.
But Waigel, under pressure from his conservative CSU to stick to a water-tight interpretation of EMU criteria, on Saturday stressed his commitment to the deficit target.
"We won't talk about decimal points. There is only one figure in the treaty, that is the (number) three," he said.

"The euro must be as stable as the deutschemark, or we can't give it to the Germans," Waigel told NTV news television, adding that any talk of softening the criteria would mean other countries would try and get into the single currency with deficits as high as 3.9 percent of GDP.

Waigel, who was to meet other EU finance ministers in Luxembourg on Sunday evening to discuss preparations for EMU, said Germany had to wait and see what position the new French government took on the issue.
He stressed, however, that French governments in the past had been consistently in favour of EMU.
Despite Waigel's denials of a debate in his party over the EMU start date, CSU board member Markus Soeder said the party would rather delay the euro than soften the criteria.

But former European Commission president Jaques Delors told Focus news magazine a delay to EMU would be disastrous. "Even only a one year delay to the start of the currency union would be the end of the project," he said.

The debate about the possibility of a delay -- until recently a taboo subject in Bonn -- flared up this week when Waigel was forced into a humiliating retreat over his plan to force the central bank to revalue its gold and currency stocks to help plug a shortfall of at least 19 billion marks ($11 billion) in his 1997 budget.

Waigel, who faces stiff political opposition from junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) on tax rises, on Saturday said he would not resort to increasing taxes to fill that gap -- at least not this year.
He said savings at both federal and state level should close the gap without the need to resort to new borrowing.
As if EMU were not enough to deal with, Waigel is also in the midst of preparing the budget for next year, a task he described as more difficult than qualifying for the euro.
Waigel told NTV television on Sunday he wants to cut spending radically and push through the privatisation of further government assets to help balance the books in 1998.
He said Bonn must make "unbelievable savings" and Kohl's ruling coalition would explore which subsidies could be cut, adding everything would have to be considered.

Waigel's plans are unlikely to be popular. Several thousand demonstrators took to the streets of Munich on Saturday in protest at Bonn's welfare policies, shouting "Kohl must go!" and criticising spending cuts being made to help Germany qualify for EMU.
